In The Opinions of the People of the Virtuous City (Beirut ed., ed. Albert Naṣrī Nādir, p. 46), al-Fārābī says of the beings beneath the sphere of the moon—that is, material beings—that “some are natural, some are voluntary, and some are composed of both the natural and the voluntary. The natural prepares the way for the voluntary and exists before it in time; the voluntary cannot exist unless the natural exists first.” This is a very clear statement that being comes before consciousness—in other words, that material existence is objective.↩︎
Al-Fārābī, The Opinions of the People of the Virtuous City, same edition, pp. 38–39.↩︎

Al-Fārābī contradicts himself on this point. His entire philosophical system is built on emanation, which necessarily rules out creation from nothing and implies the eternity of the world; this is also what the meaning of his philosophical texts themselves requires. Yet in The Harmonization of the Opinions of the Two Sages (same edition, pp. 100–104), he says that God brought the world into existence from nothing (pp. 101, 103, 104), and that the world came into being. He even calls the belief that Aristotle held the world to be eternal “an ugly and objectionable supposition” (p. 100). How should we understand this contradiction, and which of al-Fārābī’s two positions should we accept? In our view, the contradiction is apparent rather than real. It was a means of self-protection—a method Arab-Islamic philosophers of the period allowed themselves to use to an unreasonable degree. Their real views are those embodied in their philosophical theories, not the statements they make outside those theories. Otherwise their entire philosophical systems would become meaningless.↩︎

Ibid., p. 74. It should be noted that al-Fārābī understands the relation between matter and form in existing things in the Aristotelian way. When a particular form belongs to a particular matter, the form is not always absolutely form, nor is the matter always absolutely matter. A form can be form in relation to what lies below it and matter in relation to what lies above it. In the same way, matter can be matter in relation to what lies above it and form in relation to what lies below it. In the present case, al-Fārābī says that the imaginative faculty is matter in relation to what stands above it, namely the rational faculty. The rational faculty, in turn, is form in relation to the imaginative faculty because it stands above it. The rational faculty remains form, since no faculty of the soul stands above it. This is what he means when he says: “It is the form of every form that comes before it.” Elsewhere he says that the rational faculty governs the imaginative faculty and the chief sensory faculty—that is, the other faculties of the soul (p. 72). In another passage (p. 70), he says that the rational faculty is what allows us to grasp intelligible things, distinguish ugly from beautiful, and acquire crafts and sciences.↩︎

By “intelligibles,” al-Fārābī means “things whose nature is to be represented in the rational faculty. Some intelligibles are, in their own substances, actual intellects and actual intelligibles: these are things free of matter. Others are not in their own substances actually intelligible, such as stones and plants, and in general everything that is a body or is in a material body” (ibid., p. 82).↩︎

In the theory of emanation, the active intellect is the last of the ten intellects and the point at which emanation ends. Ontologically, it governs the world of earthly bodies. From the standpoint of knowledge, the active intellect “is a being whose substance is an actual intellect and is separate from matter (...) [and] gives the material intellect, which is intellect only potentially, something like the light that the sun gives to sight.” In other words, it is “what potential intelligibles need in order to move from potentiality to actuality” (same source, p. 83).↩︎

Al-Fārābī divides the rational faculty into theoretical and practical parts. “The practical was made to serve the theoretical, while the theoretical serves nothing else, but exists so that happiness may be reached through it. When happiness is known by the theoretical faculty, set up as a goal, desired by the appetitive faculty, and the deliberative faculty [thought] works out what should be done (...), and those actions are then carried out through the main powers of the appetitive faculty, all human actions become good and beautiful” (same source, pp. 86–87).↩︎

Many Qurʾānic verses say this. Among them are: “Your Lord surely knows what their hearts conceal and what they reveal” (Qurʾān 27:74); “Not even the weight of an atom in the heavens or the earth escapes Him” (34:3); “Not a leaf falls without His knowing it” (6:59); and “There is no private conversation among three people without Him being their fourth” (58:7), and so on.↩︎

We should point out that al-Fārābī and the other Arab philosophers who represent the rationalist current, like the Muslim theologians and Sufis, all begin from the principle of God’s oneness understood in terms of absolute transcendence. This is the fixed starting point they all share. Their differences lie in how they deal with the contradiction that arises between absolute transcendence and the ideological positions that force them to seek some connection between God and the world. In our view, this effort expressed their opposition to the theoretical foundation of the official ideology: the absolute separation of God from the world, which in reality reflected the principle of absolute separation between one human being and another—that is, between ruler and ruled. As we saw earlier, the Sufis establish a direct link between the world and God through unveiling and direct vision. The rationalist philosophers, by contrast, establish this link through intermediaries. The theory of emanation gave them the basis for these intermediaries—the separate intellects.↩︎

He means the first matter common to the whole natural world. Al-Fārābī’s insistence on a “common nature” shared by the celestial bodies, on a common first matter, and on an existential relation between the two points toward a view of the world as a unity. His texts on this subject suggest that he tends to ground this unity materially. In none of these passages does he refer to “essence.” Instead, he repeatedly speaks of a common “matter” passing through the celestial world in a “process” that produces the “matter” of the natural world. This matter is itself common and moves on its own within natural things through another “process” that raises them gradually from lower to higher forms “until each species reaches the highest perfection of its substance.”↩︎

Although the Aristotelian account of the relation between “form and matter” is idealist because it separates matter’s form from matter itself, its content in al-Fārābī comes closer to materialism. He describes the relation in a way that makes it appear as an internal process within the movement of matter itself.↩︎

One might ask: how can this relation work independently of every external factor when al-Fārābī ultimately traces the existence of natural things back to the celestial bodies? Our answer has two parts. First, the text we are discussing explicitly says that natural motion in existing things operates according to its own internal laws and is genuinely independent of any external factor. Second, all of al-Fārābī’s texts on the celestial bodies and the emergence of natural beings from them indicate that matter exists throughout the celestial world, that a moving “process” takes place within this celestial world—which is itself bodily—and that this process passes through stages on its way toward natural existence in our earthly world. In the chain of emanation, the first intellect necessarily brings with it the existence of the first heaven, which is material. Each following intellect in turn entails the existence of another heaven, or celestial body, down to the sphere of the moon. We also find that, in al-Fārābī’s system, the celestial bodies “are of the same kind as hylomorphic [material-natural] beings, in that they have subjects resembling the matters prepared to receive forms, and they have things like forms through which they become substances, with those things existing in those subjects” (The Virtuous City, pp. 52–53). There is therefore a material link between the celestial world and the natural world. If we also take into account the eternal character of the whole system of emanation, and al-Fārābī’s statement that the celestial bodies share with the ten intellects the fact that from the very beginning they were given the best state in which they could exist as substances, along with their quantities, shapes, and visible qualities (p. 54), we can conclude that matter is eternal. From eternity it has been moving within a continuous process of its own, passing from one stage to another until the natural world comes into existence, where the process continues in

one stage to another until the natural world comes into existence, where the process continues in new forms. In other words, al-Fārābī does not speak of matter existing apart from nature, nor does he speak here of an essence. He speaks of real matter.↩︎
We have rendered al-Fārābī’s passage with some freedom while preserving its meaning completely. See The Virtuous City, p. 63.↩︎

To make al-Fārābī’s view clearer in his own terms, it is useful to quote him: “Since one and the same matter is shared by two opposites, and each opposite exists through it, while the matter itself is no more suited to one opposite than to the other, and cannot be made to belong to both at the same time, it must necessarily be given sometimes this opposite and sometimes that one, with the two taking turns (...). A single thing therefore cannot remain forever numerically one; instead, its permanence through time is made a permanence of species. For a species to remain one, individuals of that species must exist for a time, then perish and be replaced by other individuals of the same species. This continues in the same way without end” (The Virtuous City, pp. 63–64).↩︎

The difference between the determinism of predestination and the determinism of class position is that the first cannot be changed. The second can change through the action of another class opposed to the ruling class, or when an individual changes his social position.↩︎

Aristotelian demonstration has a scientific character. Aristotle, however, does not explain the scientific or certain character of a demonstration by its conformity to formal syllogistic rules. He grounds it instead in whether the causal structure contained in the demonstration corresponds to reality. He therefore holds that each kind of being requires its own form of demonstration, suited to that kind of being, because demonstration always has an ontological side. Each type of existence, in his view, opens a particular path by which the researcher can discover what that type of existence contains.↩︎

Aristotle, previously cited source (1.10, 76a 37; 1.11, 77a 26). To say that axioms are common to all sciences means that each science uses them to establish its own particular subject matter while the axioms themselves remain general. Aristotle gives the example of the axiom that if equal quantities are subtracted from equal quantities, the remainders are equal. The axiom is general in itself, but arithmetic applies it to numbers, geometry to magnitudes, and so on (same source, 76a 41).↩︎

It is worth noting that al-Fārābī’s explanation of how we come to know the “first principles of demonstration,” including the principles known as “axioms,” comes close to Lenin’s explanation: “Human practical activity had to lead human consciousness to repeat the various logical forms billions of times before these forms could acquire the significance of axioms” (Notebooks on Dialectics, trans. Marqus, Beirut, 1971, p. 213).↩︎

On the basis of this conclusion, al-Fārābī is ahead of Descartes on the question of knowledge, especially our knowledge of first rational principles, or axioms. Descartes traces our knowledge of axioms back to reason itself. For him, knowledge begins with intuition: the mind recognizes axioms that, he says, are already present in the human soul. They do not arise from repeated experience of the external world. God places them in the human mind at birth, and reason later grasps them by itself without sensory knowledge.↩︎
The Harmonization of the Opinions of the Two Sages, p. 99.↩︎

Al-ʿAlawī quotes Hādī al-Sabzawārī (Manẓūma, Iran ed., p. 249), who says that the leading Peripatetics accepted that existence is what is produced: “that is, the effect of the cause is existence, not essence.”↩︎

We should again recall Lenin’s statement that the one property of matter whose acceptance defines philosophical materialism is that matter is objective reality—that it exists outside our consciousness (Materialism and Empirio-Criticism, Arabic ed., Damascus, 1971, p. 260).↩︎

It should be remembered that by “Peripatetics,” al-Sabzawārī means the Arab-Islamic philosophers, including al-Fārābī. We do not, however, agree with the common practice of calling the Arab philosophers “Peripatetics” without qualification. They were not all equally close to Aristotle’s philosophy. Even those most closely connected with it, such as Ibn Rushd, did not agree with Aristotle in all or even most of their views. Al-Fārābī departs from Peripatetic philosophy more than any of them. And how can they simply be called “Peripatetics” when their connection with Neoplatonism is so obvious?↩︎

The way of knowing that al-Fārābī describes here also appears in statements such as “universals [essences] are obtained from particulars” and “universals are, in truth, experiences.” This approach can be seen as an example of Lenin’s statement that the “essence of things” or their “substance” expresses nothing more than human knowledge of things—a knowledge that continuously deepens—and of his statement that essences are relative rather than fixed properties of things (Lenin, Materialism and Empirio-Criticism, Arabic ed., trans. Munīr Mashāyiḵ, Damascus, 1971, p. 263).↩︎

Al-Fārābī’s understanding of the relation between sensory and rational knowledge, as we have explained it, can be seen as an early form of understanding the dialectical relation between essence and appearance. As we see it, he was able, even if spontaneously, to approach the dialectical-materialist proposition that the senses reflect external appearances and particulars in sensory images, while the essence of phenomena cannot be grasped by the senses alone. The internal unity between a phenomenon and its essence is what makes the transition from sensory to rational knowledge possible.↩︎

His name was al-Ḥusayn, his kunya was Abū ʿAlī, and in Arabic philosophical literature he is known by the title “the Supreme Master” (al-Shaykh al-Raʾīs). He was born in 370 AH/980 CE in the village of Afshana near Bukhara. He spent his early childhood in the town of Kharmaythan, also in the Bukhara region, where his father, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sīnā, served as administrator on behalf of the Samanid ruler Nūḥ ibn Manṣūr. In Bukhara itself, Ibn Sīnā studied with private tutors in his father’s home and later continued learning through his own efforts. He tells us this in the autobiography that he partly dictated to his student Abū ʿUbayd al-Jūzjānī, who completed the account after his teacher’s death. The biography is reproduced by al-Qifṭī in Informing the Scholars of the Lives of the Sages, p. 269, and by Ibn Abī Uṣaybiʿa in Classes of Physicians, vol. 2, p. 2, where Ibn Abī Uṣaybiʿa gives Ibn Sīnā’s birth year as 375 AH. Ibn Sīnā died in Hamadan, Iran, in 428 AH/1036 CE.↩︎

In Ibn Sīnā’s time, the Arab caliphate had reached an advanced stage of division and fragmentation. During the fifty-eight years of his life, the “Supreme Master” lived while three Islamic caliphates existed at the same time: the Abbasid caliphate in the East (132–656 AH/750–1258 CE), the Fatimid caliphate in Egypt and North Africa (297–567 AH/909–1171 CE), and the Umayyad caliphate in al-Andalus (300–407 AH/912–1016 CE). Alongside these caliphates were several Islamic states linked only formally to the Abbasid caliphate: the Samanid state, with its capital at Bukhara (261–389 AH/874–998 CE); the Buyid state in Fars, Rayy, Hamadan, Isfahan, and Iraq (320–447 AH/932–1055 CE); and the Ghaznavid state, with its capital at Ghazna in Afghanistan (351–582 AH/962–1186 CE). There were also the small ṭāʾifa states in the Maghreb and breakaway principalities within these larger states, such as the principality of ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn ibn Kākawayh, a former Buyid military commander who seized Hamadan and Isfahan in 414 AH/1023 CE. Ibn Sīnā also lived through the final period of the Hamdanid emirate of Aleppo (333–394 AH/944–1002 CE).↩︎
